speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly
could not find a better beginning for the protest I desire to register against the coercive measure which the Government wishes to force through the House without consulting the people, than by reading here a resolution adopted by all the mayors of my county, at a meeting held in Vaudreuil, the county town, on June 13 last.
As for me, I find in this resolution the whole subject, matter of my speech.
Here is the resolution:
To the honourable Members of the House of Commons in Parliament assembled.
Extract from the proceedings of the municipal council of the county of Vaudreuil, adopted at its general session of the thirteenth of June, one thousand nine hundred and seventeen, literally takes as follows:
Moved by Counciller D. Bellemare, mayor of the parish of St. Lazare, seconded by Councillor Joseph E. Quesnel, mayor of the parish of Rigaud, and unanimously carried:
"Whereas the present Government no longer Minister of Canada, has just laid before the Canadian Parliament a Bill providing for military conscription for the overseas service;
"Whereas the present Government no longer hold a mandate from the people to pass such a Bill;
"Whereas this Bill is contrary to the Constitution which governs us, and to the country's traditions;
"Whereas we are governed by democratic institutions, and that the people should be consulted upon all important measures, with greater reason upon a measure which demands the blood and the gold of the nation ;
"Be it resolved that this council strongly opposes the enactment of military conscription in this country before the consent of the majority of the people has been obtained by means of a referendum ;
"And that a copy of the present resolution be sent to the House of Commons, to Sir Robert Borden and to Mr. Gustave Boyer, representative of the county in the House of Commons.
"And the petitioners shall always pray."
Given at Vaudreuil, this 16th of June, J.917.
True copy.
(Signed) J. N. Legault,
Asst.-Sec. -Treas.
This resolution was unanimously adopted by all the mayors of the county, not excepting a single one. Besides the two already mentioned in the resolution, were also present: Messrs. J. N. Lefebvre, county registrar and mayor of the village of Vaudreuil; Antoine Lalonde, of the parish of Vaudreuil; Azilda Daoust, of lie Perrot; John Me-Naughton, of Como; Galt Brown, of Pointe Fortune; Ludger Cadieux, of St. Redemp-teur; Emery Quesnel, of Ste. Marthe and James Berry, of Ste. Justine de Netvton.
Two other municipalities have no representatives on the county council, on account of their having a city charter. I am speaking of Dorion and Rigaud, but, nevertheless, I may state that their mayors would have been of the same opinion as their colleagues, at least the first mentioned, in whose name I can officially speak. And what is most noticeable in this resolution, is its moderation. It is all fair play. It simply requests that the people be given an opportunity to be heard on a measure of such importance. Another fact which deserves consideration is that this county council has three English-speaking mayors who join in this petition.
Besides this protest coming from the most authorized body of my county, I laid before this House other petitions signed 'by several thousand people. Most of these petitions had been signed at tibe suggestion of the reeve of the county, ,and they call for either a referendum or a general election, before this measure be adopted. Other petitions, from private parties, have also been sent to me and duly received, I have likewise laid them on the Table.
I may state, Mr. Speaker, that I was most happy to see such a general protest on the part of my constituents, for it encouraged me and confirmed me in the attitude I had decided to take, from the very moment this Bill was introduced.
T.he population of Vaudreuil county, Mr Speaker, is composed of peaceful people, law-abiding, fond of harmony and, above all, anxious to live on good terms with their English compatriots who cut quite a figure in the total population. And I would venture to assert that if all 'the English and French Canadians in the country c. uld agree as they do in my constituency we never would have any knotty problem to solve.
How much, therefore, do I deplore the tone upon which the present debate is proceeding. The conscription issue has been completely set aside by some hon. member's on the other side of the House, who saw fit to base their arguments upon racial grounds Truly, one might be led to believe that conscription is not a military question but rather a racial issue.

Mr. Speaker, this principle at stake does not appeal to me in such a light. To my mind, this measure is before Parliament just as all the other great questions have come before this House, but, because of its vital importance, it awakens a general interest throughout the country. On this question, the province of Quebec, among all the provinces, counts for one, no more no less, and I fail to see why some people are trying to have these proposals pivot solely around that province.
As I have just said, compulsory service is a matter of vital importance and it should not be considered from the several points of view of the two. great races inhabiting this country, but rather from the standpoint of the whole nation from the Atlantic to the Pacific, according to their opinion of its *citizens either for or against conscription. And I understand that the Liberals Who. are fighting this measure are not doing it to the aspirations of one race, hut are voicing the anti-conscriptionist sentiment, as it is to be found in every one of the nine provinces of confederation. If the French Liberal mem-*ers have stood in this House ito defend the .stand taken, by their province, it is in reply to the provocations they have been subjected to by the Conservative members sitting on your right. And I would appeal to the hon. Prime Minister's sense of justice to check the vehement out-pourings of his partisans who, by their senseless .appeals, are actually raising a rancour from which no good results can be expected.
These rumours of revolt which might arise, here .and there, in the province of Quebec should cause no undue alarm, for I am honestly convinced that the only revolt that might likely break out in this country, would be between conseriptionists and anti-conscriptionists, to whatever race they may belong. And the riot which took place in Winnipeg not more than a few days ago, bears ample evidence.
I .shall vote .against the Military Service Bill for three reasons:
Firstly, because I have no confidence in the honesty or in the ability of the present Government ;
Secondly, because this Parliament is presently sitting without any mandate but that of its own members, and therefore, has not, in the meaning of the constitution, any rightful existence ;
Thirdly, because the establishment of compulsory service is an economic error and, adopted without the people's consent, would become an arbitrary act and a menace to confederation.
In order to make good my first argument, to wit.: that I have no confidence in the

present Government, I will not lose any time in citing the long list of scandalous matters which have been charged against them, more particularly since the beginning of the war, although long previous to 1914, the Government had already made several vents in their coat of arms. Never did scandals arouse public opinion to such a degree as those connected with the supply of ammunition, equipment and all other war material. And what a pitiable defence have they not offered for every charge laid against the Government, or against some of its ministers.
The honest and independent public opinion of this country has long ago lost all confidence in the present Government. When I speak of the Government's incapacity, I am perfectly justified by what has unfortunately occurred: its unpardonable errors, its extravagant expenditure in the organization of the contingents, the grotesque and costly performances of its exMinister of Militia-its Napoleon the little, as Victor Hugo liked to nickname the last French emperor, who provoked the disaster of 1870-the exorbitant prices paid right and left for war supplies, the unrestrained squandering at the Valcartier camp; the quarrels of Camp Borden; the painQil and condemnatory report made by Dr Bruce upon the Canadian hospital's service in England, and. many other blunders the enumeration of which would by itself take up my whole time. However, the emergency is too great a one for me to exact today this rendering of accounts in connection with which the people of this country, willing or not must foot the bill. But, a matter about which the Government betrays its utter inefficiency and about which we have the right of demanding a severe and immediate accounting, is its criminal unconcern to protect the people against the vampires of every description, who are taking advantage of them and. subjecting them to the horrors of the high cost of living. Tire poor people cannot maintain that equanimity for the morrow which may keep the millionaires who sit here as ministers or as members of the present Parliament. No. the working man, whether in the mills or on the land, to whom every other day bring? trouble and uneasiness for his family and for himself, has to bear, during the terrible period we are now passing through, the adverse lot of hardships, the constant labour under the yoke, and the privations due to the lack of comfort, to the high cost of foodstuffs, of fuel, of clothing and of all the other necessaries of life.

The people who have been asked their generous and loyal contributions to this great war, the people who have answered so liberally, had at least the right to rely upon the Government's strong co-operation to be protected against the trusts of every description. I am therefore right when I charge the present Government with being unfit for the great task it had assumed, to wit.: to protect the labouring classes of this country. In the face of such facts, I am convinced that it would be unwise to let the Government venture into such a serious policy as that of adopting conscription without consulting the people, the sovereign dispenser.
My second argument is that we hold no lawful mandate and that we are sitting here solely on our own authority. In 1914, we passed an Act, the purport of which was to allow the Government to make a redistribution of the constituencies in the provinc :s, that is to say, to increase or reduce their numbers, according to their respective populations. From this fact, the representation of the House of Commons, from 221 as it is to-day will be increased to 235 at the next general election. That is to say that, since October 1910, these 14 new divisions are entitled to have a representative in this House. Under our Constitution a Parliament must never last more than five years. Now, the one elected in September, 1911, therefore ended in October, 1916.
Again, if things had been thus, that is to say, if the present Government had not believed itself indispensable to the preservation of the Empire in the first place, and to that of its political friends in the second place, we would have had elections in 1915 or 1916, and the population of this country would be now fully represented in this House. At the present date, although this Parliament has exceeded its term, of the 235 constituencies which should be represented, 23 are vacant through death or other causes of absence, and 14 are unrepresented; these being left here, as present members, to decide upon the important matter of conscription, only 198 members, when there should be 235.
In 1914, the war broke out. The Liberal party assented to a truce, in order not to hinder in >any way the work of the Government who had decided to give its full cooperation. Although, at that time, the hon. Prime Minister had before his eyes the example of the British and French Governments, where the cabinets were reorganized by the joining in of the different party
leaders until then opposed to one another, he saw nothing, and he never thought of asking the Liberal leaders to come into his government; a step which would have assured a more effective and a more honest participation.
In 1916, the Government asked for an extension of Parliament and it appears that, lest they should appear as being disloyal to the Empire, the Liberals had to give in. Jingoism had been so' heated' up that they had to consent. But it was clearly understood that the extended term which was to end in October, 1917, the Government should not bring about any coercive measure, such as conscription.
According to that agreement, this extension was unanimously voted by the House and ratified by the Imperial Government. What then has since happened that the Liberals' generosity and good faith should have been so grossly deceived? The hon. Prime Minister has declared on more than one occasion that he would not impose con-sciption. On January 17, 1916, especially, a month before the extension was granted, he spoke as follows in this very House:
In speaking in the first two or three months of this war, I made it clear to the people of Canada that we did not propose any conscription, I repeat that announcement to-day with emphasis.
He also authorized his ministers to give the same promise. The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) took advantage of it to pay his respects to the Archbishop of Montreal. The hon. Minister of Inland Revenue made all he could of it in^his Dorchester election. The hon. Colonel the Postmaster General went so far as to indulge in puzzles about conscription; in substance, he stated to the timorous voters of that division :
You need not fear conscription; in any case, should it ever be imposed upon you, you have only to cross the line.
Now then, what happened, that conscription should to-day become an ordter of the day and that the Prime Minister should mean to impose it upon the country in such a peremptory fashion, in spite of the agreement made, in spite of his own declarations, of his ministers' declarations, and at the [DOT]cost even of an unlawful act to be committed by a lapsed parliament?
Would it be that, during his last journey to London, it had been demonstrated to the Prime Minister that there was an urgent call for soldiers? Well, not so, if I can judge from the following official statement:

London, June 21.-The Canadian Associated Press is authorized to say that the attention ol Honorable Walter Long, colonial secretry, having been called to a suggestion in newspaper despatches that Sir Robert Borden had proposed conscription in Canada because he was urged to do so in the Imperial War Cabinet, he states there is not the smallest foundation for the suggestion that Premier Borden was urged to introduce conscription either in the Imperial War Cabinet or the conference. The matter was never even mentioned and the last thing the members of the home government would do is to interfere in the matter which is entirely one for Canada. Mr. Long further adds he saw' Sir Robert Borden frequently up to the last day he was here and had no idea w'hen he left he was going to propose the introduction of conscription on his return to Canada.
The hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) stated, the other day, in this House-and he must be well informed- that England had 3,000,000 soldiers on the reserve forces, and that the same country had 1,500,000 young men not yet enlisted. Quite recently, the Prime Minister asked the leader of the Opposition to join him in forming a coalition cabinet. It was somewhat late, indeed, as the war had been declared for over two years and a half. At all events, the first condition laid down by the leader of the Opposition was the withdrawal of the conscription Bill. This condition sine qua non could not satisfy the Prime Minister who, on the contrary, wanted the Opposition leader's co-operation to cloak his act. Now, if the Liberal party can be upbraided for having consented to that extension of Parliament, these facts should exonerate it. As I said a moment ago, Parliament should have been prorogued in October 1916, it has been extended for one year, that is until the month of October, 1917. Therefore, this prolongation term expires four months hence, when we should have general elections. But they are now already speaking of a further extension, for salvation, as far as the Canadian jingoes can see it, depends exclusively on the maintenance of the present Government in permanent power. No, really, did we not know the ravenous appetite of the Tories in this country, we would be led to believe that the present executive has a providential mission. Other British colonies have had their elections, New Zealand and Australia. Each and everyone of the provinces of this country have had their own. The Conservative party have felt their bitter result, and even not later than this very week, the results in Saskatchewan have disagreeably tinkled in their ears. And, nevertheless, the war did not fare any worse. Oh no, there is only Canada, 
wherein all the democratic institutions which govern us must be broken, in order to, and against the will of the people who is the sovereign arbiter, establish stringent law's which are reproved by the very large majority.
I find it strange that it should be contended by some people that the Liberals strongly criticise the Government's conduct for the simple pleasure of worrying them or of running them down and putting them out of power. But, should the Opposition be blamed for having been vigilant? On every occasion, we have denounced the scandals, as it was our duty so to do, and it was only with difficulty that the Prime Minister condescended to give sham investigations, and the guilty parties have never been troubled. All those monopolizers enjoy immunity, always under the pretense of patriotism. But why not put it the other way? That we find it strange that a Government without any mandate from the people should thus cling to power. In our country, it is war that makes the Government to hold fast; in other countries, war causes them to change as often as circumstances warrant it.
If the Liberals exact due respect for the constitution, what is there so strange in that? In all these tactics on the part of the Conservatives, it strikes me that it is not the interest they have for the Empire that inspires their action. That is only the pretext. The reason, the only true one, is that they are afraid of facing public opinion with such a disreputable record.
We are in this country ruled by a democratic government, that is to say that everything in this government is amenable to the people itself, the representatives are directly responsible to the people, and nothing can be done without the latter's approval. And that is why the parliamentary term has been limited to five years, after which the members are obliged to go before their constituents and give an account of their trust to their constituents, who are the supreme arbiters; the latter either approve or disapprove the past conduct or the future plans of their representatives.
'Therefore, every enactment of vital importance to the people should be passed upon by the people itself, just as the Liber als have done it for the Naval Service question and for reciprocity. Neither the Government nor Parliament have the right to adopt a measure setting the country towards an unknown destination, containing in itself extremely serious consequences, not only for the national unity,-I mean

the good understanding between the two great races who live in this country and which was referred to in many a speech- hut especially for the very preservation of the people's welfare. The people, in my opinion, under these circumstances, have more than any one else, the right to say if they will consent to venture into the prosecution of a policy which may lead to bankruptcy, not only the country, generally speaking, but would also infallibly fall upon the property of every inhabitant respectively-
I have heard the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) also the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), in their speeches, deny to a certain extent the sovereignty of the people, and insinuate that the latter should be governed, even contrary to its own opinion, according to circumstances, or if the Government should -see fit to do it. It is undoubtedly this same trend of opinion which caused the two hon. members for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) and of West Lambton (Mr. Pardee), who seceded from their party upon the referendum amendment and prefer supporting the conscription Bill, to state that, if the conscription issue was submitted to the people, the latter's verdict would go against its enactment.
Such an admission on the part of several hon. members leaves us in a state of perplexity. They are then disposed to make a most serious infringement to the constitution which governs us, and once entered upon that path, it will not take many years before we have in this country an autocratic government which will care for the people only pro forma. The latter will have no more prerogatives in the affairs of State, except of paying the expenditure and assuming whatever responsibilities may follow, be they good or bad.
Why extol so much the beauties of democracy, that is to say the government of the people by the people, if, upon a question of lift or death as this one, it is even refused the right to give its opinion.
In this very House, I heard not long ago two distinguished men speaking to us. One represented France, the other, Great Britain. Both of them displayed before us, in most eloquent -and wonderful terms the beauty of democracy, symbol of most absolute liberty for every people. Democracy, were we told, is the safest guarantee for the preservation of civilization, it is the doctrine of equality; but what! it is through it that is manifested the people's will which must ever and everywhere be sovereign!
Mr. Vivi-ani lives in a chivalerous country whose history is resplendent with heroic deeds. For many years past, in the statutes of that country there exists the obligation for all, rich .and poor, aristocrats or common labourer, .to rush to arms whenever the country is in danger. In the ranks of their armies, there is no caste, no privileged class, all are equal.
In England, the law did not oblige any one to take up arms, it is true, in case of war, for confident in her fleet which ensured her the supremacy of the seas and having, on the other hand, only a very restricted territory to defend1, that country, as I say, did not foresee so terrific a conflict as the one which stains with the blood o,f millions now the European continent, and which would one day compel her to send to the battle front millions of her soldiers.
Now, in these two countries, France and England, what did happen since the declaration of waT? From the very beginning the different parties hushed their combative spirit in order to have but one thing in view: the -country's preservation. All efforts were directed towards -a common end, that of victory, and for that purpose, the world has seen united in one same government the leaders of all factions who had till then been opposed to -one another. In France, the adversaries of yo-re were now fast friends; all had hereafter one sole -ambition, that of winning, of driving back the Teutonic -invasion, whi-ch forty five years of active preparations had made, not only threatening, but terrific.
And not withstanding this first concentration of the moral forces of the nation's leaders, several ministries have succeeded one another. In France, they have changed their government as often as -circumstances, always rapidly varying in this war, demanded it. And what a fine example of disinterestedness and of patriotism! Those holding power to-day would become on the morrow simple co-operators; leaving to others, without spite or resentment, the authority until then vested in them, knowing that France's destinies demanded those personal sacrifices.
In England al-so, we find similar instances of sublime patriotism on the part of the Liberal government. At the very outset, Mr. Asquith invited Mr. Bonar Law, the leader of the Opposition, and his followers, to form a National government. -Later, Mr. Asquith himself resigned to make room for Mr. Lloyd George.

thirteenth of the amount spent by England for the purchase of ammunition. Therefore, for every thirteen. million which England spends in munitions, we shall be called upon to pay one million. You will agree with me that this item will form an enormous amount, especially when you will consider that the Imperial government for munition purchases is spending by the hundreds of millions.
In 1911, under the late Administration, when Canada was in its period of progress, we expended $87,774,000 and our revenue exceeded that expenditure by several millions, which we employed in meeting the interest charges on our capital debt. Future has therefore in stock for us some hard problems to solve. Our export trade amounts to $2,000,000,000. At first sight, we might be led to believe that such an enormous figure should bring a large revenue to the Government, but that is a mistake. The clearest profit of all that trade and of all that commerce goes directly to the manufacturers and, above all, to the war contract manipulators. The profits accumulated by the munition manufacturers are exorbitant. Fortunes have been created and many an individual, who was a poor man yesterday, is to-day a millionaire. As soon as war is over, this fictitious trade will largely fall. Ask the working men of any description, who have toiled and are still toiling in the factories, how much, at the end of each week with the high cost of living, they can save? After the war, the working men will be out of work, they m.ay probably suffer privation verging on to famine, while their employer of yesterday will strut amid the gold which war industries have brought to his door. What should be done that we might usefully take part in the war? The Allies cry for food and munitions, for munitions and food. That is what we need, do they say. The English and French commissions have come to the United States, arrangements have been made, and that country has advanced them at once several thousand millions of dollars, hut not in currency, only in food and ammunition.
Is it by imposing conscription that we can better fill their wishes?
In Canada, this Government and all the provincial governments have advocated' and commended agricultural overproduction, the country places have been flooded with agricultural bulletins and pamphlets, in short,

a most active campaign was everywhere inaugurated on those lines. The result up to date has not been a marvellous one. Will it be so to-morrow? Some doubt may be entertained when it is known that farmers are everywhere short of hands, for, from the.beginning of the war, the farmers' boys, in large numbers, have gone to the cities where they were attracted by the high wages paid in the munition .shops. Here they took the places of the working men and of the other labourers who had enlisted, in the first days of the war, to escape .starvation which was then threatening the country. Indeed, we recall those armies of unemployed who made public demonstrations and cried for work. During the following year, the old shops, and new shops were opened everywhere to manufacture munitions, and they have all been filled, half, if not three-quarters of them, by men from the country places.	.
The official reports from the various provinces of the Dominion show that the lack of farm labour is already .and everywhere giving rise to serious anxieties.
I now borrow from the Avenir du Nord a compilation of opinions given by the leaders of the agricultural movement.
Mr. Arthur S. Barnstead, secretary of the Industrial and Immigration department of Nova Scotia, writes in the Gazette Agricole du Canada:
The labour problem will evidently be a most difficult one to solve in Nova Scotia, this year. We have until now depended for our labour upon the emigrating: farmers who would come here from Great Britain. Not only is this resource gone, but thousands of our young farmers are to-day overseas on active military service. The situation is far from cheerful.
Mr. W. A. Riddell, superintendent of trade and labour, in the Public Works department, of the province of Ontario, writes as follows:
Scarcity of help in Ontario is being felt just as much as in the other provinces. We have evidence of this in the following statement:
We could employ five hundred farm labourers in our locality, writes a mayor to us. The same mail contained a letter asking for a farm boy and stating: We could employ a whole load of young men in this neighbourhood.
We have five agents at work in the United States, soliciting men to come and work in Canada. The kind of help that can at present be secured in the United States for farm labour, is somewhat poor in quality.
Mr. F. Auld, Deputy Minister of Agriculture in the province of Saskatchewan, writes:
Our agricultural production will be limited, this year, on account of the scarcity of labour, and that is why we have decided to make a

special effort in order to recruit all the old farmers and all the old farm hands, to help to get in the harvest.
Special agricultural agents of this province are Just now In the United States.
Mr. H. A. Craig, Deputy Minister of Agriculture in the province of Alberta, writes in his turn:
Last winter, all those interested in the question of crop production have expressed some anxiety on account of the evident labour scarcity. The number of young men employed on farms is far inferior to what we could employ, for a very large number of young men of Alberta have enlisted for overseas service.
Mr. Wm. E. Scott, Deputy Minister of Agriculture, in British 'Columbia, writes as follows:
But the labour question is the greatest difficulty ; it is the obstacle which for the time being prevents the increase in production. The farmer perfectly Understands that it is his patriotic duty to do all he can in order to increase the food supply; he would do it, if he could get the necessary labour. It is, at this very time, a most distressing question in British Columbia and its solution is very hard to find.
We cannot expect much aid from the United States, because they are suffering from conditions similar to our own, and the farm labour is just as scarce.
It must not be forgotten that nearly 35,000 men have left the province for overseas service, since war began.
Hon. Martin Burrell, Minister of Agriculture, reminds his fellow-citizens of the importance of intensive culture, and then he
adds:
Looking towards the gloomy days which may bring this third year of the war, the hardest one yet, we realize more and more the vital importance of the food factor in the final outcome. The Government urges farmers to hold on, a matter of increasing difficulty; I do so, not in view of the rise in the prices which will undoubtedly affect every commodity, but because of the precious and most special assistance which Canadian agriculture can extend to the Empire at this critical hour.
The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett), director of the National Service, stated on February 28, that:
In ail probability, the lack of foodstuffs will be felt still more keenly before the next harvest in Great Britain, in Prance and in Italy, and as, of all the Dominions, Canada is the less distant' from those countries, the latter are naturally looking to us; they see in us their first source of supply.
The lack of labourers, did he add, is the main difficulty in the way for realizing these objects and we intend making extraordinary efforts to find the proper remedy.
And this paper most sensibly concludes:
Is that the means to accomplish, this end, by carrying on an exaggerated military mobilization, and by even imposing it though conscription?
Our agricultural start, far from being accelerated, has slackened since the war began. From 1910 to 1911, in one year, the number of sowed acres in the West had increased by 3,500,000; from 1912 to 1916, in four years, the increase has been only of 1,500,000.
And it is in the face of such a, serious declaration, Mr. Speaker, in spite of this general state of uneasiness, stated and proved by all the provinces of the Dominion, that the Government wants to impose compulsory service, that is to say, to further drain our already reduced population, to increase the difficulties created by the lack of manual labour, and to imperil our agricultural production which is of vital importance for us, for the Empire and for the Allies.
Canada's foremost duty, to-day even more than in the past, is ito increase her agricultural production, in order to provide for the victualling of the Empire and of the other allied nations whom the situation created by the war threatens with actual famine.
Let us increase our agricultural production. That is what we are called upon to do from all sides.
More than ever, in the face of present events, of the urgent calls for agricultural overproduction and of the statements of the competent men I have just quoted, I believe that the Government should let the working men remain in the cities and the tillers on their farms.
Canada has made a noble effort up to date, the part she has played is an admirable one, and for the future she should confine herself to produce and still produce.
It must also be considered that, if such a marked depopulating of our rural districts keeps going on, either for the army or for the city munition shops, it will be calculated to wholly upset our economic fabric, and expose us to incurable ills, not for ourselves alone, but also for the Allies who are clamoring for food. Where and how are we going to get it for them, if recruiting be continued with such energy, and especially if it be made compulsory, for there is no middle course possible, if you drain the shops, the labour market, the city stores; the next day, it will be the country places that will be requisitioned for men to fill the gaps.
And I could not conclude this argument in a better way than by quoting the testi-



mony of a man who should be considered as an authority in keeping with the high position he occupies:
Making use of the man power.
The question is rather one of organization than of recruiting without measure.
Under this heading, Mr.'Henry Pate, deputy and secretary of the army commission in the French Parliament, wrote, in January last, in the Paris Journal an article from which we quote the following lines which should be read and pondered over: " There is, in every effort, what one sees, for instance the keys of the Anger board, and there is what one cannot see, the mechanism. What would be, without the mechanism that commands, the war which our foes compel us to wage? Let us make up our minds to grasp the problem. Understanding the war does not consist in considering the war under its simpler aspect, recruiting exceedingly large numbers of men at the risk of imperilling the very bases of any prolonged action. Neither does it consist in adopting measures which are practically fruitless from the military point of view and which are of such a nature as to deeply perturb manufacturing and economic production."
It is intended to impose conscription; why so? It is to overcome a spreading uneasiness, to repair a failure in recruiting, or to show an untimely and inconsiderate zeal.
But before going to such an extremity, would it not be of common discretion to wisely consider if we have not, until now, .participated in this war to a reasonable extent, and in proportion to our popula tion >and to the wealth of our country? _
'There are eyes who will not see and ears who will not hear. Prom their talk, one would take it that the aid given by Canada to England amounts to naught. Let u? review the facts for a moment: the effort made and the aid given by our country during this war is something to be wondered at. Since the declaration of war, Canada has nobly done her duty, as compared to her population and her wealth. An army numbering 420,000 men of all ranks has been enlisted; 125,000 are already at the front, while 126,000 are in reserve in England. According to a report submitted by the Minister of Militia, 100,000 soldiers have already fallen on the field of honour, either killed, wounded or made prisoners. A large number, still in Canada, are only awaiting the order to embark.
All honour to the heroes who face the foe's fire! They have shed their blood upon the plains of Flanders, iat Langemarck, at Saint Julien, at Courcelette, at Vimy. Thousands of them have fallen heroically, engraving, in immortal letters on the

tablets of history, the name of our country. Let us do homage to our braves whose valiance was great, as great as the magnitude of the task they had undertaken, for it was voluntarily that they rallied to the British flag.	.
Besides all this, Canada who, before the war, had a debt of $336,000,000, will soon have one of $1,300,000,000. Add to this also, the high cost of living, in this country, which is putting every family in narrow circumstances.
Well now, in the face of this admirable participation of our country heretofore, who could take us to task for failing to do our duty? Great Britain is certainly not complaining. Then, why should the Prime Minister of this country resort to this extreme and arbitrary measure, when the most interested country, Great Britain, has not even requested him to do. so? Why so much haste in rushing the country into troubles, which can entail nothing but evil, if the country itself do not so decree it after an appeal to the people?
And I do repeat it; if, from the very beginning of the war, the Prime Minister had appealed to the Liberals and formed a national government, our effort would certainly have been more successful and at no greater expense. And we would not to-day have to resort to conscription.
Now, what is really this compulsory service bill? The Government, by this Bill, is cajoling more than one class of society, and one has only to belong to them, as all and everyone of them would be exempted from the draft. The exemption clause is so wide that it may cover all cases; for it does no.t specifically state what classes, what callings shall be exempted; it does not mention the farmer's son any more than the workman employed in the munition shops. It simply states that:	"a tribunal may decide whether it is expedient, in the national interest, that such or such a man, then appealing to it, should instead of being employed in military service, be engaged in other work in which he is habitually engaged." And in section 12 of the present Act, the Government reserves. the right to make regulations to secure the full, effective and expeditious operation and' enforcement of this Act.
We have indeed been told in the House, that the farmer's sons would be exempted, but up to what number, two, three, four, we do not know; that is in the tribunal's discretion. And the munition workers and

others who will be dismissed from the shops just before enlistment opens, will they have ceased to be useful to the national interest, on account of the arbitrary measure taken against them? These are so many open questions. But, at all events, the law shall be the same for all. As soon as the order will have been given to apply it, all those whom it concerns, class after class, according to their age and condition, will be automatically enlisted. If they wish to be exempted, they may afterwards appeal to the said tribunal.
And another point upon which I would like to call the attention of the House, is that the Bill does not specify that the Government may enlist only 100,000 men. As the Bill is framed, the Government may go up to the age limit of enlistable men. If certain fanatics were to be believed, the province of Quebec were the only province opposing compulsory service. Well, that is not proven; only a referendum could bring out the facts. Moreover, the inhabitants of that province are charged with every crime and overloaded with every /hardship; they are called disloyal /and pro-Germans, and some hot-headed people, who have evidently more belly than brains, isudh as the editors of the Orange Sentinel [DOT]and the Toronto News and notable chieftains of the Orange order, threaten us with all kinds of dire punishment. Fortunately, the sound and enlightened majority of our population know how matters stand; they are well aware that this persecution is stirred up by a boisterous minority and do not hold responsible for it the bulk of the English Canadian, And as the latter, indeed, judge the French Canadians in another light than that in which their agitating compatriots hold our race, they likewise understand that the acts of the agitators in our own midst are not chargeable to the mass of the French Canadians. It is a well known fact that opposition to conscription has been manifested from Vancouver to Halifax. Have not the English labour associations declared themselves unanimously against the measure? Upon this question of intensive recruiting, was it not Lord Shaughnessy, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, who, on March 12, 1916, made before the Montreal Board of Trade a statement somewhat as follows:	Canada has performed wonders,
but I cannot believe that (the proposal that we raise 500,000 men, is either practical or
187J	I '
possible. We have -so many- things to attend to, munitions to manufacture, lands to till, we are asked to help in feeding the British nation, and lastly, we have our financial problem to solve. By sending over 500,000 men from Canada, we would make among the labouring people of this country a gap which might bring most serious results.
And yet I believe this eminent citizen, is indeed a political friend of the Government The Government intends to enforce com pulsory military service, Mr. Speaker, and seek elsewhere the required labour; it is spending several thousand dollars advertising in the American newspapers for farm hands to fill the places of those who are gone. What said the working men of /Canada at their convention in Ottawa, on June 11, 1917?
For an efficient participation in the war, it is not compulsory service we need, and we are positively of the opinion that:
The necessities for the effective conduct of the war are:	Food, munitions, shipping and
military man power, and Canada is geographically well situated to supply the first named three essentials and can do much to assist in winning the war by developing her production of these essentials to her fullest extent.
We are strongly of the opinion that this is the best service that Canada, with her small population, can render. We declare ourselves as most emphatically opposed to the proposed conscription measure, and we urge the workers of Canada to oppose by every means in their power enactment of such legislation.
When this Bill was announced by the Prime Minister, anti-conscriptionist demonstrations took place in Montreal. Such a course was most likely in a city of 700,000 souls, where the labouring masses are numerous, where meetings of thousands of men can be called like a train of gunpowder. It is easy to understand that, in such populous centres, there should have been scuffles, even disorders, but in the country-places of the province of Quebec, everything ran its usual peaceful course; the farmers have simply voiced their protests, through their municipal 'councils or by petitions.
But what is there so abnormal, so antipatriotic, in these protests against an unpopular measure? Were not similar meetings held even in the city of Toronto, the hotbed of the purest jingoism? It is true that in this luminary-city of Canada, the principle of free speech was scorned and the soldiery did brutally break up the peaceful meeting which the common people intended to hold. In Guelph, the same thing hap-

pened, and the English citizens, who boast of their freedom in this country of Canada, were very roughly handled, by the soldiery again. In Winnipeg -and in Vancouver, likewise, popular -meetings of honest citizens, of the common people, of the men who -sweat and toil to earn their living, h-ave had a similar fate.
Truly, what -a fine civilization is that preached by a Canadian government who, to defend -a -democratic principle in Flanders, or to have the citizens of this country appreciate the full beauty of free opinion, of free conscience -and of civilization, would be ready to have their own fellow-citizens massacred right now. Therefore, it is not only in Montreal that consciences are revolting against the conscription Bill. From every part of Canada protests are coming, from Englishmen, from Scotsmen, from Irishmen, as well as from the French Canadians. But the yellow sheets of Ontario take good care to close their eyes to what is going on everywhere else, to fill their columns with filth only against the province of Quebec. Their object As most apparent, for, to have conscription passed, they think it necessary to overheat their fellowmen's patriotism by giving vent to an unwholesome hatred against the French element of this country. But, fortunately, the fair and honest element of ou-r English compatriots are not disposed that w-ay -and they let every one bear his own duties and responsibilities. In that also do we trust.
But was it not in Calgary that, at a public meeting, they sang " God save the people " instead of " God1 -save the King "?
If all the hon. members whom I have heard speaking 'in favour of compulsory service, since the opening of this debate, should likewise -be within the scope of this Act and wctc, like all those it may reach, obliged to put on the uniform -and go to the front, I am wondering if they would have spoken with the same fervour and enthusiasm. It is all very well for them to allege age, function or any of the causes of exemption included in this Bill; hut it seems to me their loyalty would show itself in -a much better light, if they gave the best proof of its sincerity, by enlisting. They should follow the example of Kerensky who has bravely put himself at the head of the Russian troops, for in the rear of the firinglines there tare positions to be filled by men of forty-five years of -age and over, by mem-

hers of the learned professions as well as by mechanics, by millionaires as well as by paupers.
And -should these hon. gentlemen, who -endeavour to increase by -compulsion the contingents already -sent to Europe give evidence of all the eagerness -and the courage to do the duty they preach to others, I aim satisfied that the example, set from so high, would induce thousands -of other brave men to do the same. And I might addi that such an example of disinterestedness would find an echo even in those who just now deny them the right to impose this coercive measure.
These remarks are addressed not only to the conscriptionist members of this House, but also to the advocates of this compulsory measure outside of these premises, who are preaching the fulfilment of a duty they are beforehand assured of being rid. In other words, they are conscriptionists less for themselves than for others.
I shall vote against the amendment to the amendment proposed By the hon. member for Berthier (Mr. Barrette). A six months hoist would not settle the question; it would only suspend for that space of time the -anguish of the country, that is all, while a referendum or a general election would settle the question once for all. If the majority of the voters of this country declare themselves -against conscription, the over-excited minds will revert to order and the country will resume with more fervor the work of efficiently assisting the Allies. If, on the contrary, the majority of the electors should vote for -conscription, there will be only one course to take, that-of 'bravely submitting.
For us, French Canadians, our sentiments are vastly different from theirs, for we have no particular attachment to France or to England. For France, we still return the remembrance of far away associations; we above all have much admiration for her. It is France herself, with her conception of beauty, with her literature, her arts, her science and her democracy that we love.
To England, we owe loyalty for the granting of the liberties we enjoy, and which permit us to live so peacefully in our homes, -for we cannot hold her responsible for our domestic quarrels embittered through the fanaticism of certain people of this country. But, our English and our Scottish compatriots in the Dominion, have more than a kindly feeling and remembrance for England; she is doubly their mother-country.

The Englishman, the Scotsman, who have emigrated at the time of the conquest have come to settle in a country which had become their own. The British flag which, upon the citadel of Quebec, took the place of the Fleur-de-lis, has never since ceased to shield them.
Our ancestors who took the oath of allegiance, and centuries have caused us to' forget later on, the one who had abandoned us, without ever remembering us. Now, English immigration, begun at the start, has always been continued uninterruptedly since then, and that is why we should not wonder nor blame our English fellow citizens for that loyalty which draws them towards the country of their origin, neither should we hurt their heart feelings. However, while admiring in our neighbours that patriotism which arms them in defence of the land of their origin, and the greatness of the cause which inspires them, I am asking myself how it is that so many of them have not yet understood that we also, the French Canadians, we .likewise feed upon an ideal of patriotism for everything pertaining to our race. The soul of our English fellow-citizen enthuses at the thought of the mother country; no one thinks of denying them that noble feeling; but they should at the same time realize that the preservation of a language by a people is likewise entitled to great respect. The Canadian of French origin has but one country, Canada, while the English, the Scottish; the Irish Canadian have each two countries. That is why, upon a question of such importance as that of compulsory service, the best means to take not to bring these elements to clash, is indeed that of a referendum, and I shall vote for it. The British Crown, in granting to the French Canadians the privileges which duly enjoys every British subject, did consequently guarantee them all the rights which this quality confers in its most absolute meaning. And is that what is happening? I say no, and that, most of the time, they have to be satisfied with what the majority feels like relinquishing to them. Whilst, in the province of Quebec, where the English are the minority, the latter enjoy under the provincial government the greatest liberty in the organization of their educational system, in the other provinces, where the French Canadians are in a minority, they only enjoy a few concessions. If the latter claim what they believe to be fair and just, if their compatriots of the province of Quebec take their part, they are aceu*ed of disloyalty and of rebellion.
Anyone who judges matters dispassionately and impartially must admit that these continuous discussions and this ostracism of the French language, in the schools of certain provinces, have only created bitterness between the two great races who divide the country between themselves.
No one admires more than I do the patriotism of our English compatriots who long for Great Britain's triumph, but how much I do wish also that they too could understand the respect they should likewise profess for a whole people who want to preserve their language.
In 1867, a solemn compact was made by the two nations, English and French. That contract 'stipulated to each its privileges and its obligations. Nothing is more sacred that the pledged word and more official than the magna charta of Confederation. Why does one of the contracting parties to this memorable document now wish, in defiance of honour and of its solemn promise, pass over and consider the Confederation Act, which guarantees the equality of the French race in this country, "as a mere scrap of paper." Is it that we are here living in Germany? Should the sons of those who have signed and approved the Act of 1867 be less honourable and less conciliating than their fathers? The latter have made <a compact, which their .sons .should in honour respect, and in .so doing, peace and harmony would'be restored in this country. And then the two great races inhabiting it, uniting their common efforts, would in mutual love and respect, work out their destinies.
On motion of Mr. Kyte the debate was adjourned.
